Social networks always have two sides, good and bad. So think carefully before you join. Some social networks have a minimum age, usually 13 years old.

Many students use social networks to connect with friends, get information, learn knowledge and skills, or share their views. But some students use them in wrong ways: posting fake news, threats, bullying,… which hurts other people or themselves. For example, a student was punished by the school for posting false information (copied from social media without checking) that worried other students; some students were stopped from taking an exam and investigated by the police for photographing the exam paper and asking others online to do it.

The algorithm in words (sorting numbers in ascending order):
  • 1. For the first position, do a loop: 1.1. Compare each number (from the second position to the last) with the number in the first position. 1.2. If it is smaller, swap it with the number in the first position. 1.3. At the end of the loop, the smallest number is in the first position.
  • 2. For the second position, do the same loop (compare from the third position to the last): the second smallest number goes to the second position.
  • 3. Do the same for the third, fourth,… positions, up to the position before the last.
  • 4. Finish: the numbers are sorted from smallest to largest.

• Carry out the solution: put the chosen solution into action. In Activity 1, the robot moves in the chosen way, like running an algorithm. If the algorithm is right, the robot finds the exit and leaves the maze.
  • Evaluate the result: look at how well the solution works, to improve it or find new solutions. For example, test the wall-following algorithm in many different mazes to improve it for special cases.
In short, problem solving has these steps: 1) Understand the problem: find what is given and what we need. 2) Analyse the problem: look at each part of the problem to find a way to solve it. 3) Choose a solution: based on the analysis, find and choose a way to solve the problem. 4) Carry out the solution: put the chosen solution into action to reach the goal. 5) Evaluate the result: check how well it works and find its strengths to improve it.
Try the four formulas of Table 10a.1 in the spreadsheet simulation: type them into cells C1 to C4 (for example type =COUNTIF(A1:A4,">100") and press Enter).

The general formula is =COUNTIF(range, criteria). range: the cells to check and count; criteria: the condition to check the cells in range. In Figure 10a.1, to know how many times money was spent on each item, use COUNTIF to count the cells in B3:B10 with each item. So the formula in cell G2 is =COUNTIF($B$3:$B$10,"Ở"), which tells how many times money was spent on “Ở” (housing). But the item name is already in cell F2, so the formula in G2 becomes =COUNTIF($B$3:$B$10,F2) (Figure 10a.2). When you copy it to G3…G10, it gives the number of times for each of the other items.
Try the two formulas of Table 11a.1 in the spreadsheet simulation (type them in cell D1).

In Figure 11a.1, in cell H2, use SUMIF to add up the money spent on “Ở” (housing). The cells to check are in the Item column, B3:B10; the condition is the item name “Ở”; the cells to add up are in the Amount column, D3:D10. So the formula in H2 is =SUMIF(B3:B10,"Ở",D3:D10). But the item name is already in cell F2, so to copy the formula correctly, the condition becomes F2 and the ranges must be absolute addresses: =SUMIF($B$3:$B$10,F2,$D$3:$D$10) (Figure 11a.2).
